# Introduction
Sarah's post for Discussion A on use of linearity for drug effects intrigued me.

# Packages
We load the required packages.
```{r label="pkg", results = 'hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse) # used to manipulate data and plot
library(ggfortify) # some extra ggplot functions
library(GGally) # pairs ggplot and other options
library(car) # many added features for regressions
library(flextable)
library(MASS) # Boston data
library(ISLR, verbose=FALSE, quietly=TRUE) # most data
```

# Data
First the raw data.
```{r}
Dose= c(2.5,5,10,20, 40,60)
Reduction = c(5.7, 6.4, 8.45,9.5,12,12.5)
```

Put into a data frame.
```{r}
sarah = data.frame(Dose=Dose, BPRed = Reduction)
```

Make the graph to check.
```{r}
ggplot(sarah) +
  geom_point(aes(Dose, BPRed), shape="triangle", size=4)+
  geom_line(aes(Dose, BPRed))+
  theme_bw()
```

Now plot the Reduxction vs log of Dose.

```{r}
ggplot(sarah) +
  geom_point(aes(log(Dose), BPRed), shape="triangle", size=4)+
  geom_line(aes(log(Dose), BPRed))+
  theme_bw()
```

Much straighter. The transformation of Dose fixed it.

Let's check the residuals by running regressions in both cases.

```{r}
sarah.fit = lm(BPRed~Dose, data=sarah)
summary(sarah.fit) %>% broom::tidy()
summary(sarah.fit) %>% broom::glance()
autoplot(sarah.fit)
```

R-squared is 87% but residuals form a hump (RF plot) and standard residuals vary wildly (SL plot).

The overall sigma is 1.09. The p-value of the overall regression is .005 or 5x10^-3. 

```{r}
sarah.logfit = lm(BPRed~log(Dose), data=sarah)
summary(sarah.logfit) %>% broom::tidy()
summary(sarah.logfit) %>% broom::glance()
autoplot(sarah.logfit)
```

The R-squared is 98%, the residuals are centered around 0, and the SL plot shows much less gain. The sigma is only .32 and the p-value for the ovewrall regression is 4x10^-5.

# Discussion
The transform makes the regression a much higher quality one, with much less variation in hte residuals, and much more predictive power.  So using the log transform is a good tool for removing the problems.

# More Insight
Why does this work?  Let's examine the original data.  
```{r}
Dose %>% as_tibble_col(column_name="Dose") %>% flextable()
```

As is common in medical experiments to find a proper dosage the dosage was approximately doubled for each level.  I maybe made a mistake looking at the original graph in picking out a dose of 4 for the first point. Perhaps it was 2.5, if so it's a direct doubling. So that is an exponential increase.  Therefore taking the log of Dose makes it into a linear variable!!!!!

So it appears that as Sarah said, increasing Dose linearly reduces BP linearly!!!!  She is absolutely right to think of linear functions as appropriate for drug effects.

And we saw that a residual graph that looks like a kind of hump shape
```{r}
autoplot(sarah.fit, which=1)
```

can be changed using a log of the independent variable to a graph more like a normal random graph with zero means like this. The range of the residuals is much smaller also, instead of from -1 to 1 it is -.25 to .25. We want residuals to be small.

```{r}
autoplot(sarah.logfit, which=1)
```


# Conclusion

We can learn a lot about transforms with a little exploration.
